Sampling isometric tensor network states with monitored quantum circuits

Yuqing Rong Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Nansha, Guangzhou, 511400, Guangdong, China    Huan-Hai Zhou Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Nansha, Guangzhou, 511400, Guangdong, China    Guo-Yi Zhu Email: guoyizhu@hkust-gz.edu.cn Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Nansha, Guangzhou, 511400, Guangdong, China    Jinguo Liu Email: jinguoliu@hkust-gz.edu.cn Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Nansha, Guangzhou, 511400, Guangdong, China
Abstract

Projected entangled pair states (PEPS) provide an efficient variational ansatz for two-dimensional quantum phases, but computing observables remains challenging because PEPS contraction is generally costly. Here, we parameterize two-dimensional quantum states using variational PEPS subject to isometric constraints and map the resulting ansatz onto monitored quantum circuits, replacing tensor-network contraction with circuit sampling. For infinite cylinders, the transfer matrix defines a quantum channel on the virtual boundary. We use a fixed-point treatment and a monitored-circuit unraveling of this channel to evaluate observables efficiently. Using a constant number of variational parameters and a number of qubits that scales only with the cylinder width, our method yields a phase diagram for the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model in qualitative agreement with DMRG results. Because the monitored circuits are compatible with near-term quantum hardware, this approach provides a hybrid quantum–classical framework for simulating two-dimensional quantum many-body systems.

1 Introduction

Characterizing the ground-state properties of interacting quantum lattice models is a central problem in condensed-matter physics. Explicitly representing the full many-body wave function quickly becomes impractical because the Hilbert-space dimension grows exponentially with system size, so practical methods must exploit the structure of physically relevant states. Tensor network states serve as a variational ansatz for many-body wave functions, decomposing them into local tensors whose virtual bond dimensions control the representable entanglement. They have become one of the main tools for describing and simulating quantum many-body systems [37, 7]. In one dimension, matrix product states (MPS) [38] underlie the modern formulation of the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) [48, 42] and allow efficient contraction and optimization. In two dimensions, projected entangled pair states (PEPS) [47, 7] are the natural extension of MPS and, at fixed bond dimension, encode area-law entanglement in higher dimensions [46, 13]. The main difficulty in PEPS is contraction, which is #P-complete in general [43, 18]. Practical calculations therefore rely on approximate contraction schemes such as the corner transfer matrix renormalization group (CTMRG) [34, 36] and boundary-MPS methods [45, 14]. Even with these schemes, contraction cost and accuracy remain key limitations.

Isometric tensor network states (isoTNS) [51] form a PEPS-like two-dimensional ansatz with local isometric constraints. The isometric constraints simplify contraction by defining an orthogonality column, which reduces local contractions to one-dimensional MPS contractions. The column can be shifted by the Moses move [51], with leading finite-size cost O⁡(D7)O(D^{7}) for fixed physical dimension, where DD is the virtual bond dimension; its infinite version extends isoTNS to infinite strip geometries [49]. The isometric structure also gives a natural connection to quantum circuits, since each local tensor can be embedded into a unitary gate acting on virtual and physical qubits [44]. This correspondence has motivated quantum-circuit approaches to tensor-network ground-state optimization [28, 26]. It also gives a dynamical view of contraction: Malz and Trivedi [32] formulated isoTNS contraction in terms of quantum-channel dynamics and analyzed its computational complexity, and Dektor et al. [10] introduced Born-rule sampling algorithms for finite two-dimensional isoTNS.

Building on these developments, we study the translationally invariant isometric PEPS (isoPEPS) geometry shown in Fig. 1(a), an infinite cylindrical spiral. Translation invariance along the infinite direction permits a fixed-point treatment: contracting successive columns is summarized by one repeated column transfer acting on the virtual boundary. The spiral geometry orders the column transfer sequentially, while the isometric constraints allow each local tensor map to be embedded in a unitary gate; together, these features yield a sequential quantum-circuit implementation. We argue that the cylindrical spiral PEPS entails only a limited loss of generality: at the cost of an increased bond dimension, it can represent a conventional cylindrical PEPS (Appendix A). Owing to the isometric constraints, this transfer matrix can also be interpreted as a completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) boundary quantum channel [32]. Its stationary state is the environment of the infinite cylindrical spiral. Computing this stationary state exactly requires storing and evolving a boundary density matrix whose Hilbert-space dimension grows exponentially with the circumference WW; the same transfer process, however, is naturally realized as a quantum circuit acting on a register of only O⁡(W​log2​D)O(W\log_{2}D) qubits.

The key insight is to unravel this boundary channel by measuring the physical qubits as each column is applied [9, 33, 39, 5]. If the measurement outcomes are discarded, one recovers the usual mixed-state channel evolution. If they are retained, the virtual boundary state follows a stochastic quantum trajectory [39, 6]. This construction is related to monitored random circuits, where Born-rule measurement records can drive measurement-induced entanglement transitions [1, 22]. Here, however, the measurements unravel a fixed PEPS boundary channel, and the records are used to sample its stationary process rather than to tune across such a transition. Under standard ergodicity assumptions, the time average of an infinite trajectory converges to the stationary boundary state [25]. Thus the measurement record both unravels the boundary channel and supplies samples for estimating physical observables, without explicitly evolving the full boundary density matrix. This distinguishes our approach from prior work in two ways: in contrast to the finite-size Born-rule sampling of Ref. [10], a single ergodic trajectory here samples the stationary state of the infinite system directly; and beyond the channel formulation of Ref. [32], the sampled record serves as the noisy objective of a closed variational optimization loop.

We implement the variational ansatz by parametrizing each local isometry as a unitary gate composed of pp repeated blocks of single-qubit rotations and entangling gates. Measuring and resetting physical qubits after their interaction with the virtual boundary allows the physical qubits to be reused during the iteration, reducing the active register size. Neutral-atom Rydberg arrays provide a concrete hardware route for these primitives; see Sec. 4.

We apply the framework to two square-lattice spin models. As a validation test, we first consider the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM), where the optimized energy density across different transverse fields agrees with DMRG and other numerical references [21, 31]. We then study the frustrated square-lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model, whose phase behavior involves competing Néel, stripe, and debated intermediate nonmagnetic regimes, including spin-liquid and valence-bond solid (VBS) scenarios [23, 16, 35]. The magnetic and dimer order parameters in Fig. 3.2 distinguish these regimes, and the momentum-resolved spin and dimer structure factors in Fig. 3.2 are consistent with them. Together, these results demonstrate that monitored isoPEPS provide a reliable framework for variational studies of two-dimensional quantum phases.

2 Method

2.1 isoPEPS as parameterized quantum circuits

We consider a two-dimensional quantum spin system on the infinite, translationally invariant cylindrical spiral of circumference WW shown in Fig. 1(a). The equivalence between this spiral representation and an ordinary cylindrical PEPS is established in Appendix A. Each site of the isoTNS [51] is an isometric tensor AA, mapping the two incoming virtual legs to the physical leg and the two outgoing virtual legs, subject to the isometry condition:

where dd is the physical dimension and DD is the virtual bond dimension. The isometric constraint ensures an exact mapping to a unitary gate, which can be viewed as a rank-six tensor after completing the isometry.

We can complete the remaining orthogonal basis of AA to obtain a unitary gate UU, which reproduces the isometry when its physical input is fixed to |0⟩\ket{0}:

U⁡(|0⟩phys⊗|ψ⟩virt)=A​|ψ⟩virt=∑s|s⟩phys⊗Ks​|ψ⟩virt,Ks≡⟨s|phys​U​|0⟩phys,U\left(\ket{0}_{\mathrm{phys}}\otimes\ket{\psi}_{\mathrm{virt}}\right)=A\ket{\psi}_{\mathrm{virt}}=\sum_{s}\ket{s}_{\mathrm{phys}}\otimes K_{s}\ket{\psi}_{\mathrm{virt}},\qquad K_{s}\equiv\bra{s}_{\mathrm{phys}}U\ket{0}_{\mathrm{phys}}, (2)

where |s⟩\ket{s} runs over the measurement basis of the physical qubit and the operators KsK_{s} act on the virtual factor. The isometry condition implies ∑sKs†​Ks=A†​A=I\sum_{s}K_{s}^{\dagger}K_{s}=A^{\dagger}A=I, so {Ks}\{K_{s}\} forms a valid set of Kraus operators; these generate the measurement unraveling of Sec. 2.2. The gate acts on nq=log2​d+2​log2​Dn_{q}=\log_{2}d+2\log_{2}D qubits—one physical factor and two (vertical and horizontal) virtual factors—so U∈S​U​(2nq)U\in SU(2^{n_{q}}).

We parametrize each gate UU as a product of pp layers, where each layer consists of single-qubit rotations Rx​(θ)​Rz​(θ)R_{x}(\theta)R_{z}(\theta) on every qubit followed by a fixed entangling pattern of CNOT gates to generate entanglement between qubits. This gives 2​p​nq2pn_{q} real parameters per gate. The resulting parameterized gate is denoted U⁡(𝜽)U(\bm{\theta}) and is shown in Fig. 1(b).

As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), columns are linked sequentially via the vertical virtual qubits, so that the output vertical virtual state of one column becomes the input for the next, forming a sequential quantum circuit along the cylindrical spiral. The total number of qubits needed is nt=log2​d+(W+1)​log2​Dn_{t}=\log_{2}d+(W+1)\log_{2}D. Translational invariance along the infinite direction allows the same gates to be reused: the ansatz repeats a unit cell of a few independent gates, whose period is chosen to accommodate the orders expected in the model at hand (specified for each model in Sec. 3). This choice balances expressivity with computational efficiency, allowing the circuit to capture ground-state correlations while keeping the parameter count manageable.

{{{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}_{\mathcal{E}}\;\longrightarrow\;\rho_{l+1}, (3)

where ρl\rho_{l} is the boundary density matrix after ll columns. If the channel is mixing, repeated application of ℰ\mathcal{E} converges to a stationary state

ℰ⁡(ρ∗)=ρ∗.\mathcal{E}(\rho^{\ast})=\rho^{\ast}. (4)

The repeated channel admits a monitored-circuit unraveling. Instead of tracing out the physical qubits in each column, we measure them and keep the outcomes. A single measurement record then defines a conditional quantum trajectory of the boundary state, while averaging over all possible records recovers the unmonitored channel evolution. Thus exact contraction and monitored sampling are two representations of the same transfer process.

Concretely, one application of ℰ\mathcal{E} corresponds to sweeping through a column of circumference WW. At site jj, we apply the local unitary, measure the physical qubit with outcome sjs_{j}, reset it to |0⟩\ket{0}, and pass the updated virtual state to the next site. Let Ksj(j)K^{(j)}_{s_{j}} be the Kraus operator of Eq. (2) associated with measurement outcome sjs_{j} at site jj, acting on the corresponding virtual factors, as shown in Fig. 1(c). Starting from ρ(0)=ρ0\rho^{(0)}=\rho_{0}, the conditional probability for outcome sjs_{j} is

p(sj|s1,…,sj−1)=tr[Ksj(j)ρ(j−1)Ksj(j)†],p(s_{j}|s_{1},\ldots,s_{j-1})=\tr\!\left[K^{(j)}_{s_{j}}\rho^{(j-1)}K^{(j)\dagger}_{s_{j}}\right], (5)

and the normalized conditional boundary state is

ρ(j)=K(j)sjρ(j−1)K(j)†sjtr[K(j)sjρ(j−1)K(j)†sj].\rho^{(j)}=\frac{K^{(j)}_{s_{j}}\rho^{(j-1)}K^{(j)\dagger}_{s_{j}}}{\tr\!\left[K^{(j)}_{s_{j}}\rho^{(j-1)}K^{(j)\dagger}_{s_{j}}\right]}. (6)

After a complete column sweep, the ordered outcomes form the record 𝐬=(s1,…,sW)\mathbf{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{W}), with effective Kraus operator

K𝐬=K(W)sW⋯K(1)s1.K_{\mathbf{s}}=K^{(W)}_{s_{W}}\cdots K^{(1)}_{s_{1}}. (7)

The probability of the full record is

p⁡(𝐬|ρ)=tr⁡[K𝐬​ρ0​K𝐬†],p(\mathbf{s}|\rho)=\tr\!\left[K_{\mathbf{s}}\rho_{0}K_{\mathbf{s}}^{\dagger}\right], (8)

and summing over all records gives the column channel

ℰ⁡(ρ0)=∑𝐬K𝐬​ρ0​K𝐬†,∑𝐬K𝐬†​K𝐬=I.\mathcal{E}(\rho_{0})=\sum_{\mathbf{s}}K_{\mathbf{s}}\rho_{0}K_{\mathbf{s}}^{\dagger},\qquad\sum_{\mathbf{s}}K_{\mathbf{s}}^{\dagger}K_{\mathbf{s}}=I. (9)

For a system with LL columns, ΓL=(𝐬(1),…,𝐬(L))\Gamma_{L}=(\mathbf{s}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{s}^{(L)}), the ensemble average over all trajectories reproduces the deterministic channel evolution,

∑ΓLp⁡(ΓL|ρ0)​ρL(ΓL)=ℰL​(ρ0).\sum_{\Gamma_{L}}p(\Gamma_{L}|\rho_{0})\,\rho_{L}^{(\Gamma_{L})}=\mathcal{E}^{L}(\rho_{0}). (10)

A single long monitored trajectory can sample the stationary process generated by ρ∗\rho^{\ast}. Under the usual ergodicity assumption for the induced quantum trajectory,

1L​∑l=1Lρl(Γ)→L→∞a.s.ρ∗.\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\rho_{l}^{(\Gamma)}\xrightarrow[L\to\infty]{\mathrm{a.s.}}\rho^{\ast}. (11)

Therefore, for an observable OO spanning cc consecutive columns, let o⁡(𝐬(l),…,𝐬(l+c−1))o(\mathbf{s}^{(l)},\ldots,\mathbf{s}^{(l+c-1)}) denote its estimator constructed from the corresponding measurement records. Averaging these estimator values along a single trajectory gives

O^L=1L​∑l=1Lo⁡(𝐬(l),…,𝐬(l+c−1)),\widehat{O}_{L}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}o\!\left(\mathbf{s}^{(l)},\ldots,\mathbf{s}^{(l+c-1)}\right), (12)

with

O^L→L→∞a.s.⟨O⟩ρ∗.\widehat{O}_{L}\xrightarrow[L\to\infty]{\mathrm{a.s.}}\langle O\rangle_{\rho^{\ast}}. (13)

Here a.s.\mathrm{a.s.} denotes almost-sure convergence. This is the trajectory-unravelling analogue of Monte Carlo sampling: a single typical monitored path samples the stationary quantum process, and time averages along that path reproduce equilibrium expectation values.

In practical simulations, the monitored trajectory has finite length, so the stationary regime can only be reached approximately. To reduce the bias from the initial transient, we discard the first lthl_{\mathrm{th}} columns as thermalization and estimate observables from the remaining LsL_{\mathrm{s}} columns,

O^Ls=1Ls​∑l=lth+1lth+Lso⁡(𝐬(l),…,𝐬(l+c−1)).\widehat{O}_{L_{\mathrm{s}}}=\frac{1}{L_{\mathrm{s}}}\sum_{l=l_{\mathrm{th}}+1}^{l_{\mathrm{th}}+L_{\mathrm{s}}}o\!\left(\mathbf{s}^{(l)},\ldots,\mathbf{s}^{(l+c-1)}\right). (14)

Each observable term is measured in the eigenbasis of its Pauli components—XX, YY, or ZZ. Measuring in different bases corresponds to different Kraus decompositions in Eq. (2) and hence to different unravelings of the same channel ℰ\mathcal{E}, whose ensemble average is basis independent. We therefore divide the post-thermalization portion of a single trajectory into sequential blocks, one per required basis—first ZZ, then XX (and YY where needed)—and estimate each Pauli term from the records of the block measured in its matching basis, as illustrated in Fig. 1(c). Because every unraveling averages to the same channel, switching the measurement basis between blocks does not disturb the stationary statistics being sampled.

The convergence rate toward stationarity is governed by the spectral gap Δ\Delta of the transfer matrix. For a gapped system, deviations from the stationary state decay as

‖ρl−ρ∗‖1≤C​e−l​Δ,\|\rho_{l}-\rho^{\ast}\|_{1}\leq Ce^{-l\Delta}, (15)

so the thermalization length scales as lth=O⁡(1/Δ)l_{\mathrm{th}}=O(1/\Delta). We diagnose this convergence by tracking representative local observables, such as the local energy, as functions of the iteration step ll, where one iteration step corresponds to adding one column. The relaxation diagnostic in Fig. B.1 shows this behavior. In this diagnostic, all trajectories are initialized from the same state, and the value at fixed ll is obtained by averaging the observable over these independent trajectories. This average can be interpreted as the expectation value of the observable in the ensemble-averaged mixed state ρl\rho_{l}. The relaxation of these observables toward a stable plateau indicates that the ensemble has entered the stationary regime, and determines how many initial columns should be discarded before performing time averages along a long trajectory. For both TFIM and J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model, we discard the first lth=100l_{\mathrm{th}}=100 steps. Fig. B.1 shows that the measured energy has already reached its stable plateau by lth≈10l_{\mathrm{th}}\approx 10 in the representative TFIM case; we nevertheless use lth=100l_{\mathrm{th}}=100 throughout as a conservative choice.

2.3 Variational optimization

The circuit parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} are optimized through the hybrid quantum-classical training loop shown in Fig. 1(d). For each candidate parameter vector, we generate a monitored trajectory from the corresponding circuit, discard the first lthl_{\mathrm{th}} columns to remove the initial transient, and estimate the energy from the remaining measurement records.

For a Hamiltonian decomposed into local Pauli terms,

H=∑αhα​Pα,H=\sum_{\alpha}h_{\alpha}P_{\alpha}, (16)

where PαP_{\alpha} are Pauli-string operators and hαh_{\alpha} are their real coefficients. The sampled energy is estimated as

E^​(𝜽)=∑αhα​𝔼𝜽​[Pα],\widehat{E}(\bm{\theta})=\sum_{\alpha}h_{\alpha}\,\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\theta}}[P_{\alpha}], (17)

where 𝔼𝜽​[Pα]\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\theta}}[P_{\alpha}] denotes the average of the corresponding Pauli-string measurement over the retained samples.

Because each sampled energy evaluation is noisy, we optimize the variational parameters using the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) [20], a derivative-free method well suited to noisy objective functions. Each candidate parameter vector is evaluated by sampling a monitored trajectory, and the resulting sampled energies are used to update the parameters for the next generation. For all optimizations, CMA-ES uses population size λ=4+⌊3​ln⁡Nθ⌋\lambda=4+\lfloor 3\ln N_{\theta}\rfloor, where NθN_{\theta} is the number of variational parameters, initial step size σ0=0.1\sigma_{0}=0.1, and at most 10001000 generations. Parameters are initialized uniformly in [0,1)[0,1) with Random.seed!(123) and constrained to [0,2​π)[0,2\pi) during optimization. After optimization, we retain the 2020 candidates with the lowest sampled energies and select the final parameters with lowest energy by exact tensor-network contraction.

3 Results

3.1 TFIM benchmark

As a validation test, we apply this method to the two-dimensional TFIM

H=−J∑⟨i​j⟩ZiZj−g∑iXi,H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}Z_{i}Z_{j}-g\sum_{i}X_{i}, (18)

where ⟨i​j⟩\langle ij\rangle denotes nearest-neighbor pairs on the cylinder, we set J=1J=1, and gg is the transverse-field strength. We optimize a 1×31\times 3 isoPEPS ansatz with bond dimension D=2D=2 and p=3p=3 repeated circuit blocks on a cylindrical spiral of circumference W=3W=3 using monitored-circuit sampling with 60,00060,000 samples. The 1×31\times 3 unit cell repeats three independent gates with A-B-C periodicity: although the TFIM Hamiltonian is invariant under translations around the cylinder, the spiral geometry distinguishes the rows within a column—in particular the first row carries the enlarged bond of the spiral construction (Appendix A)—so we allow one independent gate per row; the uniform A-A-A ansatz is compared in Table 1. Here one sample denotes one retained post-thermalization single-site measurement outcome of the monitored trajectory, cf. Fig. 1(c). We then compute the energy density of each optimized state by exact tensor-network contraction. We emphasize that sampling and evaluation play distinct roles here: the variational parameters are optimized from noisy energies estimated along the monitored measurement records, whereas the benchmark energy densities reported in this section are obtained by exact tensor-network contraction of the resulting optimized state. This comparison therefore validates the sampling-based optimization, while the accuracy of the sampled estimator itself is characterized in Appendix B. Figure 3.1 compares our energy densities with DMRG results on a 3×10003\times 1000 cylinder, obtained in this work using ITensors.jl [15] with the energy density extracted from the central bulk region. Representative literature benchmarks are summarized in Table 1. Relative to the same-geometry VUMPS reference in Table 1, the optimized energy densities deviate by 0.4%0.4\% at g=2.0g=2.0, 2.2%2.2\% at g=3.0g=3.0, and 0.9%0.9\% at g=4.0g=4.0; the largest deviation occurs near the critical region, as expected for the modest bond dimension D=2D=2. This level of agreement supports the reliability of the sampling-based optimization. Additional TFIM diagnostics in Appendix B quantify thermalization, finite-sample convergence, correlation growth, magnetization, and sensitivity to readout errors.

\captionsetup

type=figure,hypcap=false Figure 2: TFIM energy benchmark on a 3×∞3\times\infty cylinder. (a) Energy density of the D=2D=2, p=3p=3 isoPEPS after sampling-based optimization, evaluated by exact tensor-network contraction, compared with DMRG on the same W=3W=3 cylinder. (b) Relative deviation of the exact-contraction isoPEPS energy from the DMRG result, |EisoPEPS−EDMRG|/|EDMRG||E_{\mathrm{isoPEPS}}-E_{\mathrm{DMRG}}|/|E_{\mathrm{DMRG}}|. The deviation peaks near the square-lattice quantum critical point gc=3.04438​(2)g_{c}=3.04438(2) [2].

3.2 Frustrated J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model

We next apply the framework to the frustrated spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model on the square-lattice. The Hamiltonian is

H=J1​∑⟨i​j⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j+J2​∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j,H=J_{1}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\!\langle ij\rangle\!\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}, (19)

where ⟨i​j⟩\langle ij\rangle and ⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩\langle\!\langle ij\rangle\!\rangle denote nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor pairs, respectively, with 𝐒i⋅𝐒j=14​(Xi​Xj+Yi​Yj+Zi​Zj)\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}=\frac{1}{4}(X_{i}X_{j}+Y_{i}Y_{j}+Z_{i}Z_{j}). We set J1=1J_{1}=1 and vary J2/J1∈[0,1]J_{2}/J_{1}\in[0,1]. The model exhibits Néel antiferromagnetism at small J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and stripe order at larger J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, while the intermediate frustrated region has a debated ground-state character, with spin-liquid and valence-bond-ordered scenarios proposed across different numerical approaches [8, 19, 23, 16, 29, 40].

To allow the competing Néel, stripe, and period-two bond patterns within a common ansatz, we use a 2×22\times 2 unit cell with four independent gates on a cylindrical spiral of circumference W=4W=4. The ansatz uses p=3p=3 repeated circuit blocks per unitary gate and bond dimension D=2D=2, corresponding to nq=3n_{q}=3 qubits per gate and 7272 variational parameters in total.

Figure 3.2 shows the training history energy at J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5. At each training step, the energy density is estimated from Nshot=40,000N_{\mathrm{shot}}=40{,}000 measurement samples generated by the monitored circuit. The sampled energy decreases during approximately 200200 steps and then approaches a plateau. The dashed horizontal lines mark the reference result from DMRG with D=192D=192 and D=2D=2. The subsequent fluctuations around this value are consistent with the stochastic objective used by CMA-ES and indicate that the optimization has reached a stable energy within the finite-sampling resolution. For the full J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} scan, we discard the first lth=100l_{\mathrm{th}}=100 channel iterations. Quantitative accuracy is assessed in Appendix C: At J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, the D=2D=2 isoPEPS energy is 0.020.02 per site above the D=2D=2 DMRG result and 0.120.12 per site above the D=192D=192 DMRG result. Across the scan, the isoPEPS energy follows the D=2D=2 DMRG reference but remains above the more converged D=192D=192 result, with the largest deviation in the intermediate frustrated regime.

\captionsetup

type=figure,hypcap=false Figure 3: Optimization history for the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model at J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5. IsoPEPS with W=4W=4, D=2D=2, p=3p=3, and a 2×22\times 2 unit cell (7272 parameters). Each energy estimate uses 40,00040{,}000 single-site measurement samples from the monitored trajectory.

Magnetic and dimer correlations.

To distinguish competing magnetic and dimer orders, we evaluate the spin and connected dimer structure factors

S⁡(𝐪)=1Nsite​∑i,jei​𝐪⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j)​⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩,SDμ​(𝐪)=1Nb​∑i,jei​𝐪⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j)​⟨δ​Diμ​δ​Djμ⟩,S(\mathbf{q})=\frac{1}{N_{\rm site}}\!\sum_{i,j}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})}\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle,\qquad S_{D}^{\mu}(\mathbf{q})=\frac{1}{N_{b}}\!\sum_{i,j}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})}\langle\delta D_{i}^{\mu}\,\delta D_{j}^{\mu}\rangle, (20)

where the index μ∈x,y\mu\in{x,y} labels the two axes of the square lattice and μ^\hat{\mu} is the corresponding unit vector, Diμ=𝐒i⋅𝐒i+μ^D_{i}^{\mu}=\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{i+\hat{\mu}} is the nearest-neighbor bond operator along direction μ\mu, δ​Diμ=Diμ−⟨Diμ⟩\delta D_{i}^{\mu}=D_{i}^{\mu}-\langle D_{i}^{\mu}\rangle, and NsiteN_{\rm site} and NbN_{b} are the numbers of lattice sites and bonds of the chosen orientation.

The normalized order parameters M2​(𝐪)=S⁡(𝐪)/NsiteM^{2}(\mathbf{q})=S(\mathbf{q})/N_{\rm site} and MD2​(𝐪)=SDy​(𝐪)/NbM_{D}^{2}(\mathbf{q})=S_{D}^{y}(\mathbf{q})/N_{b} are evaluated at the characteristic wavevectors: M2​(π,π)M^{2}(\pi,\pi) probes Néel order, M2​(0,π)M^{2}(0,\pi) probes stripe order, and MD2​(0,π)M_{D}^{2}(0,\pi) probes columnar VBS order. The choice of dimer observable is guided by the real-space correlations: the dimer pattern occurs on vertical (yy-oriented) bonds and alternates along the yy direction. We therefore analyze the vertical-bond dimer structure factor SDy​(𝐪)S_{D}^{y}(\mathbf{q}) and use its normalized value MD2​(0,π)M_{D}^{2}(0,\pi) as the dimer order parameter. In contrast, M2​(0,π)M^{2}(0,\pi) is the magnetic order parameter used to detect stripe order. The alternatives SDx​(𝐪)S_{D}^{x}(\mathbf{q}) and MD2​(π,0)M_{D}^{2}(\pi,0) would probe a horizontal-bond pattern or modulation along xx, neither of which is observed. This directional selection is natural on the W=4W=4 cylinder, where the xx and yy bond directions are inequivalent and the geometry can pin the columnar orientation. The corresponding real-space bond-correlation patterns are shown in Fig. C.3 of Appendix C. As in the TFIM benchmark, the variational parameters are optimized from sampled energies, whereas the correlators entering S⁡(𝐪)S(\mathbf{q}) and SDy​(𝐪)S_{D}^{y}(\mathbf{q}) are evaluated by exact tensor-network contraction of the optimized state over 2121 consecutive columns, exploiting translational invariance. Since the peak height of a structure factor grows with the number of columns included, these quantities serve to identify the ordering wavevectors rather than as converged order-parameter estimates.

Figure 3.2 traces the three order parameters across J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and distinguishes three regimes. At small J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, M2​(π,π)M^{2}(\pi,\pi) dominates. In the intermediate window J2/J1≈0.5J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.5–0.60.6, both magnetic components drop sharply while MD2​(0,π)M_{D}^{2}(0,\pi) peaks, identifying a columnar VBS regime. At larger J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, M2​(0,π)M^{2}(0,\pi) dominates and the dimer signal is suppressed. The isoPEPS results qualitatively agree with the DMRG calculations performed in this work: both show the suppression of Néel order, an enhanced dimer signal in the intermediate window, and the onset of stripe order at larger J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, although their amplitudes do not coincide point by point. Figure 3.2 shows the same evolution in momentum space at J2/J1=0.0, 0.5, 0.6, 1.0J_{2}/J_{1}=0.0,\,0.5,\,0.6,\,1.0. For visualization, the Fourier sums are evaluated on a dense momentum grid, although the W=4W=4 circumference allows only qy=0,π/2,π, 3​π/2q_{y}=0,\,\pi/2,\,\pi,\,3\pi/2 as transverse crystal momenta. The spin structure factor S⁡(𝐪)S(\mathbf{q}) is concentrated at (π,π)(\pi,\pi) for J2/J1=0J_{2}/J_{1}=0, is suppressed through the intermediate window, and shifts to (0,π)(0,\pi) at J2/J1=1J_{2}/J_{1}=1. The dimer structure factor SDy​(𝐪)S_{D}^{y}(\mathbf{q}) peaks at (0,π)(0,\pi) for J2/J1≈0.5J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.5–0.60.6 and is featureless outside this window, consistent with Fig. 3.2.

The J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model tests the framework in a frustrated regime where physical consistency across competing correlations is essential, and the momentum-resolved magnetic and dimer structure factors (Fig. 3.2) together with the three order parameters (Fig. 3.2) show that the framework remains reliable beyond simple models like the TFIM.

4 Discussion

We present a variational framework for studying two-dimensional quantum phases with isoPEPS on an infinite cylindrical spiral, in which one column of the tensor network defines a quantum channel on the virtual boundary degrees of freedom. The framework builds on the isoTNS ansatz [51, 49] and its quantum-channel interpretation [32]; its central idea is to unravel this channel into monitored quantum trajectories, so that after thermalization a single long trajectory samples the stationary boundary state, and the same measurement record yields Monte Carlo estimators for observables. For the TFIM, the energy densities of the sample-optimized states agree with DMRG benchmarks and results from the literature. For the frustrated J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model, the method captures the crossover from Néel to stripe correlations and a vertical-dimer signal in the intermediate regime.

A natural next step is gradient-based optimization for this ansatz. We use CMA-ES here because it copes well with noisy sampled objectives, but its cost grows quickly with the number of parameters. Gradients obtained from the fixed-point channel or from trajectory-based estimators could allow the method to scale to larger bond dimensions and wider circumferences.

The framework should also extend to other lattice geometries, with the kagome lattice as an immediate target [50]. Gapped topologically ordered phases [24, 27] are another promising direction, since the measurement record may offer diagnostics that complement standard order parameters and entanglement-based probes.

Neutral-atom Rydberg arrays are a concrete platform for monitored trajectories: optical tweezer arrays provide programmable two-dimensional geometries and Rydberg-mediated entangling gates [4, 12], while recent neutral-atom processors have demonstrated mid-circuit readout, feed-forward, and reconfigurable circuit operations [17, 3]. The practical performance will depend on the overhead of repeated measurements and resets and on the number of samples required to estimate observables accurately; a simple independent-bit-flip model of readout errors and its effect on the TFIM energy estimator are examined in Figs. B.3 and B.3 of Appendix B.3. In such a hybrid implementation, quantum hardware generates the monitored trajectories while a classical optimizer updates the variational parameters, providing a direct path from the present simulations to experiment.

Relabeling cxc_{x} as bx,3b_{x,3} gives exactly Eq. (21). Hence

|ψsp⟩=|ψcyl⟩.|\psi_{\rm sp}\rangle=|\psi_{\rm cyl}\rangle. (25)

The spiral geometry is therefore an index reshuffling of the cylindrical PEPS: only one horizontal bond, here the first-row bond, must be enlarged from DD to D2D^{2} to carry the original closing index. The same construction extends directly to circumference WW by carrying the closing bond bx,Wb_{x,W} in the enlarged first-row horizontal index and replacing it with the spiral link γx:(x,W)→(x+1,1)\gamma_{x}:(x,W)\to(x+1,1).

Appendix B TFIM diagnostics

This appendix collects diagnostics that support the TFIM benchmark in Sec. 3. We first characterize thermalization and finite-shot convergence, then examine the correlation length, local correlations, and magnetization across the field range. We finally test the sensitivity of the sampled energy estimator to a simple readout-noise model.

B.1 Energy dynamics and sampling convergence

Figure B.1 shows the thermalization of the ensemble-averaged local energy from a common initial boundary state. The approach to a stable plateau provides an operational diagnostic for choosing the thermalization length lthl_{\mathrm{th}}: the initial columns are discarded until the curves no longer display a systematic transient. Figure B.1 presents a representative finite-shot convergence analysis for the TFIM at g=3.0g=3.0, showing the expected 1/N1/N decrease of the estimator variance.

\captionsetup

type=figure,hypcap=false Figure 7: Energy dynamics and sampling convergence for the TFIM. B.2 Correlation and magnetization diagnostics

Figure B.2 shows that the transfer-matrix correlation length grows as the field approaches the crossover region and decreases at larger gg. The maximum is shifted and broadened relative to the bulk critical point gc≃3.04438​(2)g_{c}\simeq 3.04438(2). This difference is expected for the finite circumference W=3W=3 and modest bond dimension D=2D=2, so the curve is used as a qualitative correlation diagnostic rather than a precise estimate of the thermodynamic critical point. Figure B.2 complements the transfer-matrix analysis with directly sampled, short-range observables. Together with Fig. B.2, it shows that the crossover is visible in both the transfer spectrum and local real-space correlations. Figure B.2 shows a smooth crossover from longitudinal polarization, measured by |Z||Z|, to transverse polarization, measured by |X||X|, as the field increases.

\captionsetup

(a) Correlation length ξ\xi for circumference W=3W=3, extracted from the transfer-matrix spectrum of the sample-optimized isoPEPS and compared with DMRG on the same cylinder and an infinite-PEPS reference obtained using PEPSKit.jl [30]. The vertical dotted line marks the bulk square-lattice critical point gc≃3.04438​(2)g_{c}\simeq 3.04438(2) [2]. (b) Connected correlations C⁡(r)=⟨Zi​Zj⟩−⟨Zi⟩​⟨Zj⟩C(r)=\langle Z_{i}Z_{j}\rangle-\langle Z_{i}\rangle\langle Z_{j}\rangle for nearest-neighbor pairs, C⁡(1)C(1), and next-nearest-neighbor pairs, C⁡(2)C(2). (c) Longitudinal and transverse magnetizations: |Z||Z| decreases as gg increases, while |X||X| grows toward saturation.

B.3 Readout-noise sensitivity

To estimate sensitivity to measurement errors, we independently flip each recorded measurement bit with probability pp before constructing the energy estimator. At g=3.0g=3.0, Fig. B.3 shows that this symmetric readout-error model biases the measured energy density upward. Figure B.3 shows that the corresponding absolute deviation grows approximately linearly over the tested range p=0%p=0\%–5%5\%. This calculation characterizes noise sensitivity only; no readout-error mitigation is applied.

(b) Absolute deviation |e⁡(p)−e⁡(0)||e(p)-e(0)| from the zero-error energy density. The deviation grows approximately linearly over the tested range p=0%p=0\%–5%5\%.

C.1 Sampling variance

For the Heisenberg model at J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, we quantify the sampling uncertainty of the energy estimator using 200200 bootstrap resamples for each shot count NshotN_{\mathrm{shot}}. Figure C.1 shows the expected approximate 1/Nshot1/N_{\mathrm{shot}} decrease of the variance. The fitted prefactor sets the sample count required to reach a target statistical precision.

Variance of the energy estimator versus shot count NshotN_{\mathrm{shot}}, obtained from 200200 bootstrap resamples. The dashed line is the fit Var⁡(E)=a/N\operatorname{Var}(E)=a/N with a=0.296a=0.296.

C.2 Energy-density benchmark

Figure C.2 compares the D=2D=2 isoPEPS energy density with DMRG results at bond dimensions D=2D=2 and D=192D=192. The isoPEPS curve has the same broad trend as the D=2D=2 DMRG result across the scanned frustration range but remains above the more converged D=192D=192 energy, with the largest difference in the intermediate frustrated regime. The comparison therefore indicates that finite bond dimension is a significant limitation of the present ansatz and should be accounted for when interpreting its quantitative accuracy.

\captionsetup

type=figure,hypcap=false Figure 11: Energy per site versus frustration ratio J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} for the Heisenberg model. Energy densities of the D=2D=2 isoPEPS ansatz and DMRG calculations with bond dimensions D=2D=2 and D=192D=192. The isoPEPS result shows the same broad trend as the D=2D=2 reference, while the lower D=192D=192 energy displays the remaining finite-bond-dimension error, most clearly in the frustrated intermediate regime.

C.3 Real-space bond correlations

Figure C.3 shows the nearest-neighbor spin correlations obtained by the optimized D=2D=2 isoPEPS. At J2/J1=0J_{2}/J_{1}=0, antiferromagnetic correlations occur on both bond orientations, consistent with Néel order. In the intermediate regime J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5–0.60.6, the strongest antiferromagnetic correlations form alternating vertical bonds, revealing the columnar dimer pattern probed by MD2​(0,π)M_{D}^{2}(0,\pi). At J2/J1=1J_{2}/J_{1}=1, vertical bonds remain antiferromagnetic while horizontal bonds become ferromagnetic, consistent with stripe correlations.

\captionsetup

Exact-contraction values of ⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle for the optimized D=2D=2 isoPEPS at J2/J1=0.0J_{2}/J_{1}=0.0, 0.50.5, 0.60.6, and 1.01.0, with J1=1J_{1}=1. The bond colors encode the sign and magnitude of the correlations. Alternating strong antiferromagnetic vertical bonds appear at J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5–0.60.6, while the small- and large-frustration panels display Néel- and stripe-like patterns, respectively.
